en: Preface to the *Heart Sūtra* in a Single Thread:
Alas for this mind! It is the seed of Buddhahood and the root-stump of karma. When opened, the myriad phenomena flourish;
when firmly grasped, not even a speck of dust remains. How wearying it is!
Old Śākyamuni pointed east to speak of the west for forty-nine years, yet he never uttered a single word.
Being soundless and odorless, neither form nor emptiness, when Bodhidharma questioned him, he did not recognize it; he simply faced the wall like a fool.

Throughout the generations, the patriarchs have emerged and submerged themselves, speaking of the true and the false, yet in the end they were headless dragons and snake-tailed serpents—leaving one in doubt.
If one were to kill those who permit the heroic, how many spirits would be buried? Yet suddenly encountering them, they remain as before—eyes askance and noses straight.
At that time, during the assembly at Prajñā, they were reduced to seven pieces and eight fragments by that yellow-faced old fellow. What was he saying?
He spoke of the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the twelve spheres, and the eighteen realms—an uncuttable tangle of complications. Indeed, there was.
From among the six hundred fascicles, there emerged an unconventional man called Avalokiteśvara, who spoke several "no" words to Śāriputra.
How joyful it was that he swept away all traces and extinguished all vestiges! Thus, the *Heart Sūtra* was transmitted to China and left behind for the world.

The Imperial Preface composed by His Majesty Emperor Taizu Gao, et al.: Herein, because the Dharma Master Cunkong questioned me on this matter, I could not avoid composing a circumstantial commentary;
for the sake of the public, I have set it forth and titled it "A Comprehensive Commentary on the Heart Sutra. Furthermore, I have troubled the venerable Mr.
Cun to embellish it with Japanese script and carve it for publication to be disseminated throughout this land for the instruction of beginners. Should those of clear vision [encounter it],...
To behold this is enough to provoke a laugh; "Ei!"—one must by no means let it pass, for only then is it attained.

Thus the preface was written in the autumn of the *Jōhō* year *Eishi* (1648) at the guest quarters of the Left Hall of Kōfuku-ji in Nagasaki, at the Mappō-ji branch of Hōkōzan Gokoku Shōke Ryūshō-ji, established by imperial decree from Nanto (Nara).
The Monk Yizheng, in his humble effort to verify and renew himself, respectfully records the structural outline and meaning of the *One Thread through the Heart Sutra*.

Regarding the Fivefold Profound Meaning (*wǔzhòng xuányì*) that the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai first established at the very beginning of his commentary on this sutra: [...]* *Note: The provided source text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*
This is because its essential meaning is easy to understand. Furthermore, I have categorized its text according to topical divisions (*ko*), as its structural boundaries are easy to discern.

When I frequented lecture halls, I observed that among the various commentaries and topical outlines (*kośu*) on the various sutras, this sutra alone possessed such comprehensive meaning and concise phrasing;
yet, although there were many who provided annotations, few had attempted to categorize it. Consequently, students could not avoid [this difficulty].
To be mired in seeking the ink-traces is to become entangled and lose their single thread of unity.

Now, without measuring my own limited vision, I shall emulate the ancients and categorize them, so that beginners may derive meaning from these categories; having derived the meaning, they forget the words; having forgotten the words, they embody the Truth;
having embodied the Truth, they harmonize with all things; and having harmonized with all things, they attain the single thread of unity—is this not indeed relying upon the written word?
Arising through contemplation, illuminating through contemplation, and realizing the true mark—thus are the three types of *prajñā* fully present!

Nevertheless, this primarily applies to those of middling and inferior faculties; as for those of superior capacity and sagely wisdom, they give rise to sudden faith and inclination before even unrolling the scroll:
with the precious sword of the Vajra King brandished horizontally beneath their heels, they shatter all manifold complexities in a single stroke.

To depart with such lofty dignity—how joyful this is! What need is there to speak of texts, contemplation, the true mark (*dharmatā*), form and emptiness, or even the three categories and seven elements, bodhi and nirvāṇa?
This is truly one who upholds *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate*.
If you have not yet reached this state, for now simply follow the liturgical procedures and seek the scriptures; they will reveal themselves of their own accord.
On a day when words were forgotten, someone said: "The World-Honored One preached the teachings in response to the capacities of beings;
from the beginning, he had no intention of composing formal sections. To now rigidly compile these fragmented fragments—is this not a form of attachment?
I replied: "What words are these? The Buddha is the Dharma King, possessing mastery over the Dharma. Though it appears otherwise, there is naturally a meaningful integration within it. Therefore..."
In this land, the teachings are proclaimed with fervor; the words, phrases, and meanings spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods of time coincide perfectly without exception.
How could this be a matter of intentional conformity?

Furthermore, in my own land, from the Han and Wei dynasties onward, even among those of worldly wisdom, the scenery, songs, and rhymes found in villages and alleys unexpectedly accord with the Huangzhong pitch.
The musical tones of Dali also possess the four structural principles of *qi* (introduction), *cheng* (development), *zhuan* (transition), and *he* (conclusion);
if this is so even for worldly wisdom, how much more so for the Buddha’s wisdom? Question: Was this sutra spoken by the Buddha or by a bodhisattva? Answer:

According to Shi Hu’s translation, the World-Honored One was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, having entered the Samādhi of Profound Radiance, and spoke the *Samādhi-sūtra*. Upon hearing this, Śāriputra made his request.

Question: This was spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; it is thus like the meaning of the Dharma King Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū preaching the Dharma at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the sixteen princes then preached it in turn.
Therefore, one knows that this sutra is the essential core of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the Great Chapter) and is indeed the Buddha’s own teaching.

Although the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is extensive, spanning six hundred fascicles, there is nothing within it that does not explain the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
Entering this sutra and synthesizing its contents, there is nothing that is not fully contained therein. This sutra takes a single dharma as its name because it lacks a human metaphor;
it takes true emptiness and the real mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence because it empties all dharmas;

it takes "contemplating and seeing" (*vipaśyanā*) as its thesis because one sees through illumination; and it takes "deliverance from suffering" as its function because it can eliminate all suffering. It is Mahāyāna.
Because Prajñā is the teaching aspect and shares the same flavor [as the principle], its other profound discourses are extensively recorded in various commentaries;
they are not described here for fear of prolixity.
△ This sutra is divided into three major sections: first, the Section on Establishing the Meaning; second, the Section on Exegesis; third, the Section on the Secret.

The Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom: A Single-Threaded Explanation. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree during the Tang Dynasty. The division of the structure consists of two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the text. First, the explanation of the title: *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra-ekagrantha-śāstra*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree during the Tang Dynasty.
The Monk Yizheng of Mingchu Huguo Temple, who has unified the ancient commentaries on the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"Prajñā" means wisdom; "pāramitā" means reaching the other shore, or as it is also called, crossing to the other shore.
Its meaning is profound and far-reaching, so it was left untranslated [as a compound]. "This shore" refers to saṃsāra; "that shore" refers to nirvāṇa.

The shore is the state beyond, while the middle of the stream represents afflictions; by employing wisdom as an oar to cross over, this is called "the perfection of wisdom for crossing to the other shore.

According to various sutras, śāstras, commentaries, and sub-commentaries, there are dozens of ways of explaining the meaning of *prajñā*, yet all are nothing more than provisional designations established by the Sages for the purpose of guiding and transforming beings. Therefore, it is said: "It is merely by means of provisional names."

In guiding sentient beings, if one interprets the meaning of "deliverance" (tú) by adhering rigidly to conventional explanations, then one must realize that birth-and-death is itself nirvana, afflictions are themselves bodhi, wisdom is itself ignorance, and ignorance is itself liberation. Furthermore, how could one speak of "deliverance" in such a context?
Therefore, following the present sutra and inferring from it, this is precisely the application of effort in the practice of profound contemplation.

This is its name. It is because at the moment the Mahāyāna exerts its power, it is detached from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), transcends all distinctions between ordinary beings and sages, does not fall into discursive thought, and is not based on contrived reflection;
thus, while there is nothing by which it can be named, it is given a provisional name and called *prajñā*.
*Pāramitā* is the title for awakening; awakening is precisely reaching the other shore.
To reach the principle of awakening, the essential lies in single-mindedly upholding the "empty seal" (kōin), proceeding directly and entering straight on.

Suddenly, one kicks open the sturdy barrier of the five aggregates and brushes away the illusory cataracts of form and emptiness. Thus, one attains the state where empty space is pulverized and the great earth sinks flat;
the two eyes are opened wide, and one no longer perceives what is true or false, nor what is holy or ordinary. Indeed, there is no birth.

When cessation can no longer be apprehended, when stainless purity can no longer be differentiated, when the Four Noble Truths can no longer be cultivated, when ignorance can no longer be exhausted, and when the attainment of wisdom can no longer be grasped—this is the realization of Nirvana. At such a time, even the Buddha does not know its name;
why then do we insist on calling it *pāramitā*? Reaching this stage, one calls *prajñā* "ignorance."
One may call it *pāramitā*, and one may also call it birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);
one may call it this shore, and one may also call it the other shore. Having no fixed preference and no aversion, names are established according to circumstances.
Therefore, it is said: "The Buddha’s teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* is not [inherently] *prajñāpāramitā*; it is merely named *prajñāpāramitā*."
The "mind" (*citta*) is the very essence of *prajñā*; thus, *prajñā* is simply another designation for the mind.
To claim that this sutra represents the "mind" of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Daipin*) is incorrect, as the original text does not state this.
This sutra has been translated five times in our land of China, with titles that differ slightly but whose meanings do not vary. There is a version titled *Prajñāpāramitā*...
The *Mahā-prajñāpāramitā-mantra-sūtra* exists in a version titled the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-buddhamātṛ-sūtra*, which generally refers to the "Great Wisdom Mind.
It is now named the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* according to the translation by Master Xuanzang. Regarding the term "sūtra" (*jing*):
it means a "path" (*jìng*). Since practice must proceed by way of a path, it is so called; furthermore, it signifies "constant" (*cháng*). *Prajñā*...
Because it is neither severed nor extinguished, and because it is also traversed, it is said: "One must pass through this very place before one can attain it.
It is also said: "This sutra is profound, firm, mysterious, and remote; no one is able to reach it. Furthermore, that which is spoken by the benevolent kings and the worthy sages is called a *sūtra*;
it weaves together the world and the five constant virtues. Therefore, that which is spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is called a *sūtra*, for it weaves together the principles of the universe.
Because the Ultimate Way is true and eternal, it is "unified by a single thread," just as a thread passes through flowers.
Thus, the Buddha’s spoken teachings are like the chaotic falling of flowers in the sky; the intended meaning they convey is like the thread that runs through them.

Since the *Śūramgama-sūtra* is expansive and its scope is all-encompassing, I fear that readers might see the flowers but lose sight of the thread. Therefore, I have used topical outlines (*ke-lun*) to guide them, hoping thereby to...
The *Sū* (Commentary) is so named because it "seeks" (*sou*) and "penetrates" (*tong*).

It seeks out the profound and subtle meanings hidden within the topical sections and penetrates the narrow boundaries of the winding channels, thereby ensuring that the water flows without obstruction; hence it is called the *Yiguàn Sū* (Commentary on the One Thread).
△ Next, the explanation of the text is divided into four sections: first, identifying the person who practices; second, introducing the dharma to be practiced at its time;
third, clarifying the essence by means of the cause and the school; and fourth, revealing the power and function based on the dharma.

These four major sections constitute the "Section Establishing the Meaning" (Liyi-fen), which establishes the essential purport of this single sutra. From "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" up to "delivering one... [the text continues].

The *Sarvapāpadharmanirghātanamantra* (The Mantra for Eradicating All Evil) in one fascicle contains the entirety of the Heart Sūtra. The following section provides a detailed commentary on the preceding text;

therefore, it is categorized as the "Explanatory Section. Question: All other sūtras contain the formal statements of the introduction (*nidāna*), the main body (*śarīra*), and the dissemination (*pariṇāmana*).

Why is this sūtra devoid of them? Answer: It is because the translator favored brevity. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "At that time, the World-Honored One was at [Vaiśālī]... [and so forth].
Having entered the profound Samādhi of Radiance on Vulture Peak Mountain and finished expounding the samādhi, Śāriputra addressed Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"If there are those who wish to study and practice this profound Dharma-gate of Prajñāpāramitā, how should they study it?
This constitutes the introduction; now, in this sutra, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara provides the answer.
This is the authentic core; the remaining sections on its circulation are fully contained within the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, as detailed therein.

First, the practitioner who performs this is mentioned: Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Regarding "Avalokiteśvara," there are two explanations: first, referring to the Lord of Transformation from his own perspective; second, pointing to another [manifestation]. If...
Whether oneself or others, there is no one who is not a practitioner. It is as if Śāriputra were to say:
"If anyone wishes to cultivate the Dharma-gate of Prajñā, they need only look at that person Avalokiteśvara. He does not observe with objects, nor does he observe with wisdom;
because he observes by means of observation itself, he has attained sovereignty. This is what is meant by: 'If one can hear and uphold it, what Buddha would not be attained?'"

From the moment one hears this teaching and enters the contemplation of "forgetting the object" through hearing, until the extinction of birth and death and the manifestation of quiescent cessation, one attains great mastery;
for this reason, the name is bestowed. As for "Bodhisattva," it is a Sanskrit term meaning *bodhisattva*;

in Chinese, it is translated as "sentient beings with the mind of enlightenment" (*daoxin zhongsheng*) or "enlightened sentient beings" (*jue youqing*). Thus, anyone who gives rise to the six perfections and the myriad practices [is so called].
Those who possess the awakened mind and sentient beings alike are addressed by this very name. △ Second, the sequence of the Dharma to be practiced:
"When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*..."
"Practice" refers to the wisdom that is capable of practicing; "profound *prajñā*" is the dharma that is practiced. This dharma is deep, firm, and remote;
it is not something that can be entered by the superficial wisdom of a beginner.

Therefore, it is said that the time of "practicing the profound" is not a time of seasonal hours, but rather the time of "precisely this very moment. *Prajñāpāramitā* is as explained in the preceding note.
△ Third, clarifying the essence by means of the cause and the thesis:
to perceive that the five aggregates are all empty.
To see through such illumination is called taking the cause and effect as the thesis; by breaking down the aggregates to reveal emptiness, one attains the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Because it constitutes the essence, it is categorized as the "cause" (hetu); the thesis (pakṣa) reveals the essence, and through contemplative insight (pratyavekṣā), one breaks through the silver mountain of the five aggregates (skandha) to perceive the nature of True Suchness (tathatā).
Now, as for the "aggregates," the Sanskrit term is *skandha*, which in the Tang language means "coverings" (*yin*);
this refers to the five kinds of coverings, such as form (*rūpa*), because they shroud the true void (*śūnyatā*) and thus prevent one from penetrating through to it clearly.

If one seeks within the nature of the aggregates—which are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the true and eternal—there is absolutely nothing to be found regarding coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death;
how much less so for the five aggregates? Therefore, it is said that they are all empty. △ Fourth, revealing the power and function of relying on the Dharma.
"To deliver all from suffering and calamity.

"To deliver" means to cross over. "All suffering and calamity" refers to sentient beings dwelling in this world of five turbidities, subject to the retribution of a land of rubble and thorns, entering the retribution body of a sack of the four elements, and pursuing hatred.
This is merely because the mind of consciousness falls into the pit of craving; every movement of body and mind is nothing but suffering and distress.
As can be known from the traditional teaching of the eight sufferings, all these sufferings arise from the domain of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which cover and conceal one’s nature.

Greed and anger mount like mountains, while delusion and attachment form an ocean, thereby severing the path to the Great Way. Now, by relying on the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the Prajñāpāramitā, [one may transcend them].
Revealing the celestial nature of Dangyang, one kicks down the mountains of greed and anger and dams the seas of delusion and craving.
With this single path, serene and free from obstruction, what suffering could there be? This is the power of Prajñā, by which one attains ultimate liberation in Nirvana;
therefore, it is categorized as "Acting in Accordance with the Power of the Dharma. The Section on Establishing the Meaning concludes.
△ Second, the section of explanation, which has three parts: first, explaining that the five aggregates are all empty; second, analyzing and explaining the word "empty" to demonstrate true emptiness;
third, explaining how one transcends all suffering and calamity. First, explaining that the five aggregates are all empty, which has two parts:
first, calling out the names; second, the formal explanation. First, calling out the names.
Śāriputra. Śāriputra was the Buddha’s foremost disciple of great wisdom. Because his mother’s name was Śārī, he is called the son of Śārī;
he is also named Śarīraputra (Son of the Body) and Kātyāyanīputra (Son of the Tawny One). The meaning of these names can be understood from this sutra.
It is precisely because wisdom breaks through the five aggregates that it is precious. Subhūti, wishing to explain the preceding passage, calls out the name [of the Buddha] and addresses him.
II. The Explanation of the Address (consists of two parts): 1. Explaining that the aggregate of form is itself emptiness; 2. Showing that the other four aggregates are not different [from it]. A.

Explaining that the aggregate of form is itself emptiness (consists of two parts): 1. Explanation by means of inference (*anumāna*); 2. Explanation by directly perceiving the essence (*tattva*). i. Explanation by means of inference.
Form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form.
How is this explained? It is because the preceding passage merely stated that one contemplates and sees that the five aggregates are all empty;
however, as the function of contemplation is subtle and difficult to understand, it is further elaborated upon in this second section.
To enable you to awaken through the written word, I say: "Śāriputra, I have taught that the five aggregates are all empty. Why is this?
Furthermore, I shall instruct you by means of the single character "form" (rūpa); once you understand this, the rest will be known.
For this body composed of the four great elements is originally but a delusory manifestation arising within the midst of true emptiness, just like the vision of the eyes.
The flowers in the sky manifest from the exhaustion of labor, arising within emptiness and ceasing within emptiness; therefore it is said that "form is not different from emptiness.
Since form arises in dependence upon emptiness, one should know that emptiness is the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of form. Once form is seen as form, then emptiness is likewise not empty;
therefore it is said that "emptiness is not different from form. This is an explanation through the inference (*anumāna*) of form and emptiness; hence it is called "not [different]."

The distinction between emptiness and non-emptiness does not consist in the essence of form or the absence of form; rather, it is explained through the provisional means of mutual implication and relative opposition between emptiness and form.
△ Second, the explanation by beholding the essence:
Form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
This is pointing directly at the essence itself. When it is said, "Śāriputra, I say that form and emptiness are not different," this is spoken by way of analogy;

do not be deluded by the meaning of analyzing form to enter into emptiness, nor wait for form to perish in order to manifest emptiness, thereby falling into the views of the Lesser Vehicle. In reality, the substance is such that form is emptiness and emptiness is form.
What is form? Observe this body composed of the four great elements: although it possesses the hundred bones and four limbs, there is nothing that is not form.
Even as one examines this very form—the hands dancing, the feet stomping, the exhalation and inhalation—and seeks its trace from within, not even a shadow can be found;
how much less so the substance of form itself! Is this not precisely what is meant by "form is emptiness"?
Furthermore, one contemplates this principle of emptiness: looking, it cannot be seen; listening, it cannot be heard; yet it pervades all things and cannot be discarded.

Once its presence within all things is realized, then the hundred bones and four limbs, the dancing of hands and leaping of feet, and the exhalation and inhalation of breath—all are nothing but material form moving within.
Yet, if one seeks that emptiness itself among them, it is utterly unattainable. Moreover:
Is it not that emptiness is itself form? Since the form of the body is thus, all other forms are likewise so.

Therefore, the Buddha taught that the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and even the mountains, rivers, the great earth, light, darkness, form, and emptiness—all are the eternally abiding, wondrously bright, immovable, and all-pervading nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous True Suchness. You merely use the characteristics of form and emptiness to displace one another.
They contend over the Tathāgatagarbha, yet the Tathāgatagarbha accordingly manifests as form and emptiness, pervading the Dharma-realm.
When observing its characteristics, they are fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out; when observing its nature, it is fundamentally true—merely wondrous, enlightened clarity.

Since this mind of wondrous, enlightened clarity was originally neither water nor fire, it is said that "form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form. △ Second, the integration of the four aggregates.
They are not different.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
One should understand that feeling is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from feeling; feeling itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is feeling.

The term "not speaking" is used here as an abbreviation. These four [aggregates] arise because one falsely identifies with the body composed of the four great elements and the mind that is but a shadow following the objects of the six sense-fields.
When one perceives external objects, there is sensation (*vedanā*); when one engages in mental activity and deliberation, there is perception (*saṃjñā*);
when thoughts and memories flow on like a succession of waves, it is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); and when seeds are stored within, one dies according to one's karma.
That which arises is called consciousness; all these are falsely grasped as having form based upon the physical body. Since they are immediately empty, how can the four aggregates be established?
Therefore, it is just like the aggregate of form discussed previously. II. Distinguishing the character "empty" (k'ung) to reveal true emptiness (chen-k'ung):

A. First, indicating the essence and characteristics of true emptiness. B. Second, distinguishing the wondrous nature of true emptiness as not being empty. C. Third, directly explaining true emptiness.
"There are no all dharmas. This first indicates the essential nature and characteristics of true emptiness.

"Śāriputra, these dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness" further establishes the essential nature and characteristics of true emptiness by means of the word "empty" from the phrase "the five aggregates are all empty."

This introduces the following passage: It is as if one were to say, "Śāriputra, when I speak of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as all empty, do you suppose that by emptying those five aggregates there remains some other dharma that can be emptied?
Little do you realize that if the five aggregates are empty, then all dharmas are empty;
if all dharmas are empty, then the absolute reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is fully revealed; and once the absolute reality is fully revealed, one realizes true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
There is also its essential nature and characteristics. △ Second, distinguishing the subtlety of true emptiness that is not empty:
it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
This refers to emptying all phenomena; yet, if one clings to the view of a stubborn emptiness, one will become addicted to emptiness and stagnate in quiescence, failing to...
Because one abandons [the truth] and becomes like a withered sprout or a rotten seed, it is further taught that six "no"s are spoken to reveal the wondrous nature of emptiness that is not empty.

What is meant by "non-arising"? At the very moment a single thought arises, if one turns back to contemplate the essence of this arising, one does not perceive a nature that can give rise [to anything], nor does one perceive an objective state that is given rise to.
Although there is the perception of arising, in reality there is no arising; therefore it is called "non-arising.
Just as at the very moment a single thought is about to cease, one does not yet perceive a cessation departing for some other place; therefore it is called "non-ceasing.

Arising and ceasing, ceasing and arising—these are all the principle of perpetual generation within the purity of nature. How could true emptiness possess any emotional nature? This is the Way of the Confucian.
This means that nature (*xing*) is the principle of the constant generation of emotion (*qing*), while emotion is the intentionality of the constant generation within nature.
Nature is fully present in emotion, and emotion contains nature; when nature moves, it is emotion, and when emotion is still, it is nature.
Since these two phenomena of nature and emotion cannot even be heard of as distinct entities, how much less can there be birth and extinction to be analyzed? Therefore, it is said: "Words..."

The false manifests all that is true and false; thus, truth and falsity are equally two forms of falsity. Since it is difficult to distinguish between truth and falsity, how can one discern arising and ceasing?

Therefore, it is said: "Neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure. Furthermore, within a single thought-moment of a person, there is nothing that does not possess the three dharmas of good, evil, and neutral.
This is the law of nature; thus, even when one does not intentionally think of good...
One should contemplate that what is neither evil nor non-evil is itself good; yet if one contemplates neither good nor evil, one falls into the murky state of *avyākṛta* (non-defined).
Now, the division of defilement and purity based on the two dharmas of good and evil follows their source.

Furthermore, at the very moment a single thought of evil arises, there are immediately greed, anger, ignorance, craving, guile, deceit, and lewdness—the face flushes with shame and the body becomes agitated.
To speak with deceitful and perverse words is the arising of cultivated evil; this is what is called "defilement.

Although this defiled mind is indeed evil, it is certainly not the true, eternal nature, for it arises dependent upon conditions. If it were truly existent, why would one, at the very moment of its active arousal, fail to perceive its inherent nature?
One cannot perceive the presence of evil sound or foul odor [as an intrinsic quality]. Therefore, it is said: "No."
If a single thought of defilement arises, yet at the moment one gives rise to goodness, there is affection for kin and respect for the worthy;

one maintains sincerity, restrains deviance, speaks with compassion, uses gentle tones, and walks with calm composure and slow steps. The mind is refreshed and the body feels light; this is the purity born of wholesome karma.
However, although this wholesome mind is pure, it is certainly not the truly eternal Dharma, for it arises from conditioned conceptualization. Why is this so?

If wholesome objects appear before the mind, one sees the Buddha, hears the Dharma, and gives rise to thoughts conditioned by the wholesome; perceiving that there is a pure mind, these wholesome objects are present.
If such wholesome objects are absent, the mind is not in a state of purity, and is therefore called "impure. This explanation is given in contrast to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
As for this state of being neither defiled nor pure: were one to sit within the gate of the patch-robed monks (*śramaṇa*), cutting off both paths of good and evil and trampling them underfoot—
At the very crux of birth and death, one voids excrement and urinates directly upon the crown of Vairocana; what defilement or purity could there possibly be to distinguish?

Regarding the teaching that there is neither increase nor decrease—that which existed of old does not increase in the sage, nor does it decrease in the ordinary person—if we were to discuss this in terms of "sage" and "ordinary person," one might say that while it is impure in the sage, it is not defiled in the ordinary person. This is because...
Although the Sage is a sage, his sagehood consists merely in the union of wondrous clarity—neither extinguished nor arising—with the Tathāgata-garbha;

yet the Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity that perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm. Because it extinguishes dust and unites with enlightenment, it simply gives rise to the nature of the wondrous, enlightened clarity of True Suchness.
Within this nature, how could there ever be any increase? And as for sentient beings...

Because of delusion and confusion, one turns one's back on awakening and unites with the sensory dust; thus, the toil of worldly dust arises, and there are the obstructive characteristics of the mundane world.
Yet, how could there ever be any decrease in the fundamental nature? Therefore it is said: "The sage possesses the dharmas of the sage, yet the sage does not know he possesses them;

the ordinary person possesses the dharmas of the ordinary person, yet the ordinary person does not realize they possess them. When the ordinary person realizes what the sage knows, they are identical to the sage; when the ordinary person realizes what the sage knows, they are identical to the ordinary person.
Because one is identical to the Sage, one knows that the nature of consciousness is equal to empty space; it manifests according to the dimensions of its vessel.
If the vessel is square, the space is also square; if the vessel is round, the space is also round. Yet how could empty space itself possess squareness or roundness?
Thus we know that when the mind emerges from its vessel, how could it not be sagely? Alas! The subtlety of True Emptiness is ultimate; it is truly beyond the reach of words.
When Shih reached this point, he unconsciously threw down his brush and laughed, saying: "This very life is it! It is defilement! It is increase!
What more can be said of 'neither arising nor ceasing,' 'neither defiled nor pure,' or 'neither increasing nor decreasing'?
He then struck himself once and said: "I have added one more speck. △ Third: Directly explaining that true emptiness is devoid of all dharmas. Part One: No ordinary beings.
Now, the Dharma is twofold: first, there is no dharma of ordinary persons; second, there is no dharma of sages. Regarding the fourfold [absence]:
first, there are no five aggregates; second, there are no six sense bases; third, there are no six sense objects; fourth, there are no six consciousnesses. First, there are no five aggregates.
Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
From this point onward, eleven instances of the word "no" sweep away the dharmas of both the holy and the mundane to reveal the empty nature of all phenomena.
This is as if saying: "Śāriputra, when I speak of the empty nature of all phenomena, it is because..."
The essential nature of true emptiness inherently possesses the wondrous quality of remaining unchanging while following conditions;

therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] responds to the minds of sentient beings according to the scope of their cognition. In its actual principle, not a single dharma can be found, much less the five aggregates;
hence, it is said to be "non-existent. △ Second, the non-existence of the six sense bases.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
What are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) that are non-existent? To speak of the eye-base first, the others may be understood accordingly:
when the eye perceives form, it exists because of light; if light does not come, the mere eye does not see. Since there is no light...
Coming to see is also not non-existent; if the nature of seeing were non-existent, how could one see darkness?
Seeing brightness, seeing darkness—brightness, darkness, and form are all equally the wondrous substance of True Suchness (tathatā). Because of brightness and darkness, the eye’s seeing arises;

because of the conditions of the eye’s seeing, there is brightness and darkness. Since both brightness and darkness are non-existent, upon what does seeing depend? Know that when one perceives brightness...
If one is identical with light and darkness, then one is identical with darkness; if identical with space, then one is identical with space; if identical with form, then one is identical with form.
How could there be a "eye-base" (*cakṣur-āyatana*) that can be divided? Since there is no divisible eye, the same applies to all five sense organs.
Therefore, within emptiness, there is certainly no reality to the six bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatanāni*). △ Third, the absence of the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣayāḥ*).
There are no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas.
Since the six sense organs do not encounter the six sense objects, although hearing and seeing are distinct and clear, they are none other than the single reality of the true nature.
Just as a bird flying through the sky leaves no trace and an echo from a valley produces no sound from the rock, though these things exist, they have no substantial reality. △ Four: Non-existence.
The six consciousnesses.
There is no eye-element, up to and including no mind-consciousness-element.
This is the absence of the eighteen elements; for it is because the eye and forms serve as conditions that eye-consciousness arises, and thus there are the eye and forms.
The three types of consciousness establish their respective domains without confusion; thus, the eye does not distinguish sound, and color does not intersect with hearing.

Because the natures of these consciousnesses differ, each is divided into its own domain. Therefore it is said: "Originally relying on one brilliant spirit, it divides into six harmonious combinations.

Thus there are the eighteen realms formed by the triad of the three [roots, objects, and consciousnesses]. Now, since the sense organs and their objects no longer exist, the nature of consciousness does not...

Because [the conditions] have not arisen, there is no realm of the six consciousnesses. △ Second, the absence of precious noble dharmas, which has two parts: first, the absence of precious dharmas; second, the absence of noble dharmas.
First, the absence of wise dharmas, which has two parts: first, the absence of pratyekabuddha dharmas; second, the absence of śrāvaka dharmas.
Originally, there is no Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas;
there is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance, and so on, up to neither old age and death nor the exhaustion of old age and death.

This is the absence of the twelve links of dependent origination. Once the three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements] have been completely swept away, one attains the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), yet the dharmas still remain.
Because you have not yet fallen away from attachment to dharmas, I have swept out all the dharmas practiced by the sages and saints so that you may attain the emptiness of dharmas.
Thus I said, "Śāriputra, you should know that all the aggregates, bases, elements, and sense-fields I previously spoke of are entirely non-existent.
Yet, because your view of dharmas has not been forgotten, you still think that all these dharmas were spoken by the Buddhas.

The gates of reality truly exist as that which can be cultivated and realized; yet, because one clings to them within the recesses of the mind, it is difficult to penetrate their principle of emptiness.
Have you not heard the Buddha’s teaching: "That which is called the teaching of the Dharma is itself not the teaching of the Dharma; it is merely designated as the teaching of the Dharma"?

It is just like the twelve links of dependent origination practiced by the Pratyekabuddhas; although there are three [turns] taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, [the essence remains the same].
Relying on [these teachings] is no more than using yellow leaves to stop a child's crying;
in reality, one must thoroughly understand the actual substance of self-nature, wherein not even a single word can be added, let alone hundreds of thousands of dharma-gates. Therefore it is said:

"The mark of the cessation of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words. For instance, regarding the teaching that ignorance conditions formative action (*saṃskāra*), [it is understood that] ignorance and...

The true suchness and the substance are like a second moon; because it is difficult to distinguish between the true and the false, it is said: "If the true were not truly true, I fear delusion; therefore, I have never openly expounded this.
It is solely because of the initial lack of awakening that the mind suddenly stirs, becoming the cause for the formation of the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*).

This is due to the fault of the "awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*). Because of this clarity, the objective realm is established, and from the arising of the perceived aspect (*dṛśya-bhāga*), the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) is subsequently established.
The arrangement of the differentiated aspects of phenomenal dust is called ignorance; through non-awakening, it gives rise to the three subtle states.

With objective realms as conditions, the six coarse delusions are extended. Since these are fundamentally without cause and attachment is itself delusion, attachment is precisely ignorance, while non-attachment is liberation.
Once one awakens to the principle of true emptiness, like the bright sun shining in the sky, how could there be any ignorance?
Thus, from the dark and profound gloom of ignorance (*avidyā*), wind arises and moves without ceasing, like the continuous succession of waves;

this is called "conditioned by ignorance, there is volitional formation" (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskāra*). When these formations arise, they possess the mechanism for generating consciousness; therefore it is said, "conditioned by formations, there is consciousness" (*saṃskāra-pratyaya-vijñāna*).
By virtue of this nature of consciousness, one enters the womb and dwells therein, relying upon the two drops of red and white [semen and ovum] to form name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

"Name" refers to consciousness and mind; "form" refers to material substance. Therefore it is said that consciousness conditions name-and-form. Because this name-and-form exists, there are the hundred bones and four limbs.
The eye is like a cluster of grapes; the ear is like a newly curled leaf; the nose is like two hanging melons; the tongue is like a crescent moon just after it has been bent down;
the body is like a waist-drum; the forehead is like a dark chamber. When these six features are complete, one sees.
Because the nature of consciousness is established through its entry [into the womb], it is said that "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases.

Furthermore, from the time of birth until the eyes encounter forms, the ears encounter sounds, and so forth—the mutual contact of these six locations—it is said that "the six sense bases condition contact. Upon contacting these six objects, one experiences their beauty or ugliness, which constitutes sensation (*vedanā*).
Because one feels attraction toward what is beautiful and aversion toward what is ugly within the conscious mind, it is said that "sensation conditions craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).
Craving and greed do not cease; thus, grasping arises. Because there is grasping, it is said that "craving conditions grasping.

Through this grasping and attachment, one does not escape the twenty-five states of existence in the world; therefore, it is said that "grasping conditions becoming. Since becoming exists, it inevitably invites future birth;
therefore, it is said that "becoming conditions birth. Once there is birth, there must be old age and death; therefore, it is said that "birth conditions old age and death."
Old age and death, death and death, birth and birth, life and death—these are all due to the delusive thoughts of ignorance arising for a single moment.
Because one undergoes birth through delusion and undergoes extinction through delusion, like the up-and-down motion of a waterwheel, the twelve links of dependent origination are formed.
If there were no ignorance, then the eleven [links] would be cut off at their source; therefore it is said that "when ignorance ceases, everything ceases" within the nature.
If one seeks for wisdom or folly within space, neither can be found; how much less so ignorance (*avidyā*)?

Since ignorance does not exist, what is there to be extinguished? Therefore it is said: "There is also no extinction of ignorance. Alas! How great is the fault of ignorance! Should the practitioner not be cautious?
△ Second: There is no Dharma of the Śrāvakas.
There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path;
this is the absence of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. "Suffering" refers to the retributions received according to karma within the twenty-five states of existence across the three realms.
"Origin" refers to the creation of karma through the eighty-eight latent tendencies and one hundred and eight afflictions within the three realms.

"Cause" refers to the extinction [of afflictions], which is the attainment of the partial truth and the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) by emerging from the four abodes.
"Path" refers to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), namely the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, faculties, powers, and bases of psychic power.

Since these are the actual causes, actual fruits, actual practices, and actual realizations for those within the triple world, they are called the Four Truths (*catuḥsatya*). As for "Truth" (*satya*):...

This is indeed so. For within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Great Vehicle’s ultimate emptiness, there is fundamentally no suffering to be known, no accumulation to be severed, no cessation to be realized, and no path to be cultivated; hence it is said that there is "nothing. Why is this?

Because for one who has attained the true nature (*bhūtatathatā*), even when entering the midst of the most wretched conditions, there is nothing other than a single physical body (*rūpakāya*) through which these experiences are received—let alone this physical body itself.

In emptiness, what suffering could there be? It is from a single thought of affliction that [suffering] arises; yet if one turns back to contemplate the nature of affliction, it is fundamentally true emptiness.
Arising as an illusion, it perishes as an illusion; the true mind remains unchanging—how, then, could existence be accumulated?
As for the partial truth that is realized, why is it further said that the "transformed city" is not real? It is just like this:
The place where the treasure is found is also the field of true emptiness and quiescent extinction; for ten thousand kalpas it has never been moved, nor has it ever been departed from.
What path is there to be realized? Those who possess the Way have established expedient means as counteractive dharma-gates—like seeking butter in a dream by employing various expedients.
Once the dream is broken and the object forgotten, what further use are these expedients? Therefore, although there is no path to be cultivated, [expedients are employed].

It is thus; one must reach that ground before it can be attained. One must not proceed in such a haphazard manner, lest one later regret it when it is too late to remedy. △ Second, there is no holy Dharma.
There is neither ignorance nor attainment.

Wisdom is the merit of practice possessed by Bodhisattvas; attainment is the merit of cessation realized by those who have achieved it. If there is no wisdom within the cause, the Way will be difficult to refine;
if there is no attainment at the level of the fruit, Nirvana becomes a fallacy. Such is its true reality (*dharmatā*).
Within this principle, the Buddhas of the three periods have never permitted even a single eye to gaze upon it; how could there be so many verbal designations and habitual tendencies?
As the ancients said: "Knowing such a matter, one simply rests. When cultivation and realization are both forgotten and stillness and illumination are non-dual, what wisdom could possibly attain it?
△ Third, explaining the phrase "crossing over all suffering and calamity," part five: first, concluding the preceding section.
The first [section] concludes the preceding and introduces the subsequent: there are three types of persons who, relying on the Dharma, transcend suffering and realize the truth;

third, it cites all Buddhas who, relying on the Dharma, attained self-realization to demonstrate that the Dharma is not falsely taught; fourth, it praises the profound depth of Prajñā; fifth, it combines this with the previous phrase "delivering all from suffering.
The first [part] concludes the preceding and introduces the subsequent.
"Because there is nothing to be attained.
This concludes the preceding section; it is because one relies on the fact that all things are unattainable that one realizes the bliss of true permanence.
Thus, we know that the phrase "letting go over a precipice and taking responsibility for oneself" is by no means applied lightly. △ Second, citing the scriptural basis.
The Dharma is for those who realize the truth through the exhaustion of suffering.
Because Bodhisattvas rely on the Prajñāpāramitā, their minds are without hindrance; because they are without hindrance, they have no fear;
far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, they attain ultimate Nirvāṇa.
Is this Dharma-gate of Prajñā not, indeed, the wordless *huatou*? Why is this so?
It is because this Dharma-gate is like an insipid iron sorrel dumpling; by chewing it over and over again, one completely vomits out all former evil knowledge and views.
Suddenly, one chews through the root of the tongue and turns the skin of the face inside out.
Only then does one come to know that this Dharma is not obtained from others;

it cannot be raised up nor cast down, cannot be grasped nor discarded, and though ten thousand anxieties and a thousand thoughts are like snow melted by boiling water, only a Bodhisattva can practice it accordingly.
Thus, the mind attains freedom from obstruction, such that even in times of calamity or haste, no trace of its arising can be found—is this not Nirvana? Therefore...
It is called ultimate *nirvāṇa*. △ Third, citing the self-realization of all Buddhas according to the Dharma to demonstrate that the Dharma is not spoken falsely:
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Bodhi: it is by relying solely on this seal of emptiness that one realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in the past, present, and future;
furthermore, all people are sealed with this very seal. How could this not be a non-erroneous teaching? △ Fourth, praising the profundity of Prajñā.
Profound.
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra,
an unsurpassed mantra, and an unequaled mantra.
Therefore, know that this Dharma possesses both the provisional and the real, illumination and function; it can grant and it can take away, it can kill and it can bring to life.
It depends solely upon the individual’s own willingness to accept it. Because it can give rise to sudden, resolute faith and crush the armies of Māra, it is called the "Great Divine Spell.
Because it illuminates and shatters all phenomena as empty, it is called the "Great Brightness Spell. It is non-arising.
Because it extinguishes the opposition between defilement and purity, it is called the "unsurpassed mantra. Because it ultimately reaches nirvana, it is called the "unequaled mantra.
To speak in accordance with principle, it cannot be otherwise than this. Furthermore, how shall one explain the single character "mantra" (zhou)? The verse says:
Two mouths have but one tongue; even the Buddhas find it difficult to distinguish and explain. Within the teachings, they forcefully clarify this:
a tortoise is called a turtle.
(This fifth line connects with the previous phrase, "Saving all from suffering and calamity.")
"It can eliminate all suffering.
Yet, Śāriputra, although I previously stated that it delivers one from all suffering and distress, you remained doubtful and did not believe;
only upon reaching this point have you come to know that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas benefit themselves and others by delivering them from suffering.
It is said that there are none who realize the Truth who do not rely on the power of this Prajñā; this concludes the section on the "Explanatory Interpretation.
△ Third, the Section on the Secret Conclusion, which has two parts: first, [the section] up to the exhortation to arouse faith; second, the actual exposition of the secret of Prajñā.
The Dharma encompasses all words and letters. From the beginning up to the entrustment, it inspires faith;
it is true and not false.
Among the five modes of speech spoken by all Buddhas, that which is now being taught is the true speech and the real speech of all Buddhas.
The quality of speaking truthfully—neither deceptive nor inconsistent—is also included therein; those who hear it should practice with deep faith.
These two correctly explain the secret dharma of Prajñāpāramitā, encompassing all its written expressions.
Therefore, it is said that the Prajñāpāramitā mantra is as follows; the mantra is recited:
*gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
As for me, in explaining this sūtra, I have never failed to measure it by means of intellectual understanding nor to seek its meaning through the lens of my own cognitive views. Thus [I have spoken].
In every commentary, the presence of the two characters "youyu" (猶曰) indicates that the meaning was grasped through hesitation and deliberation;

however, regarding this mantra, one reaches a point where it can only be suspended upon the wall of the mouth, and thus it is categorized as the secret dharma of Prajñā, for which there is nothing to be explained.
Why is this? It is because the dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of Prajñā cannot be entered through words, letters, or intellectual principles.
It is also valued for being preserved and put into practice so that one may personally realize its essence; therefore it is said:
"The mark of the cessation of all phenomena cannot be proclaimed in words. Yet, how is it that people of the world value words more than practice?

Thus, when our Buddha, the World-Honored One, first attained enlightenment, he walked beneath the trees and contemplated for twenty-one days, reflecting upon how the Buddhas of the past had all taught [this].
Because he expounds the teachings of the Three Vehicles, he manifests the mark of the broad and long tongue to explain such profound and subtle principles as those that are neither dry nor impure;
this is done so that those of middling and inferior capacities may be led into the gate of faith. Therefore it is said:
"Where there are only words, there is no real meaning. When speech has reached its ultimate limit, he then opens his tongueless mouth.
To expose the roots of the teeth and utter the mantra is called a "spell" (*dhāraṇī*);
it is like a vajra-ring or a thorny bramble that causes one to be unable to swallow or spit it out. This may truly be called the ultimate proclamation of Prajñāpāramitā.
Whenever I see commentators, some annotate it by taking it as the name of a deity, while others annotate it as a secret military command.
Regarding the statement that the *gongluo* (wasp) prays over the *mínglíng* (caterpillar), although this is a parable, it is likely not the definitive meaning;
however, the analogy of King [Bimbisāra] requesting *saindhava* comes closer to the actual sense.
That I have now set it aside without providing an explanation has its own reasons. If the incantation possesses such a meaning, why did the translator not translate it?
Indeed, these five reasons for not translating are precisely the direct pointers within the teachings that serve as the shortcut to the Three Vehicles.

Furthermore, how can one explain this principle? By what means of thought can one enter this gate of contemplation? If one can single-mindedly uphold this mantra, then...
Without relying on cessation (*śamatha*), one is eternally tranquil; without relying on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one is eternally illuminating—is this not indeed a saving of effort?

Therefore, the Tiantai school does not produce a mantra apart from this. As for the Vinaya school, the Buddha established the regulations of light and heavy offenses, permissions and prohibitions, and the maintenance or violation of precepts for all seven assemblies of followers;

The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (Luo-ti-mu-xie) designates its ten grave and forty-eight light precepts as the "Dharma-gate of the Ground of the Mind" (*citta-bhūmi-dharmamukha*) and also refers to them as the "Vajra Jewel Precepts of Radiance";
these constitute the Mahāyāna precepts. Subsequently, for Rāhula, he expounded the ten śrāmaṇera precepts;
furthermore, due to the assembly of the group of seven bhikṣus and others, he established the two hundred and fifty precepts for the sake of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Riding upon this, one binds the body and returns to the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*). Those who transgress have no choice but to repent by means of mantras;
is this not taking the mantra as the precept? Therefore, this mantra does not appear in the Vinaya school.
As for the Pure Land school, the Buddha expounded the sixteen contemplations to Lady Vaidehī, enabling her to transform her defiled mind.
In establishing the Pure Land, it begins with the sun disc suspended as a drum, which is the wheel of the light of the mind;

Therefore, "Immeasurable Life" refers to the Dharma-body that is neither born nor extinguished, and the "crystal ground" refers to the ground of the mind that is transparently luminous and penetrating. How could there be an external Buddha-land to be attained?
This is to know that the Pure Land is but the nature of one's own mind, and Amitābha resides solely within a single thought-moment of the person themselves.

It is because sentient beings have many divergent paths of deluded thoughts that the Western Quarter is pointed out as the singular path for focused recollection; this is nothing other than the convergence of all phenomena into the One.
Furthermore, it is because Śrī-Ābhāsvara did not enter through the "Perfect Penetration" (yuan-tong) that one is instructed to recite the Buddha’s name with a single mind.
Therefore it is said: "If one recollects the Buddha and contemplates the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.
This means that by using the name of a single Buddha, the delusions of manifold paths are dissolved, allowing one to enter directly into Bodhi.
If this were the case for all mantra-holding, how would it differ from Amitābha? For this reason, the Pure Land school does not produce mantras; [this is the distinction of] the Mantra school.
This is because the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma comprises the four teachings—sudden, gradual, secret, and indeterminate—which universally encompass all capacities of sentient beings.

To take secret teaching as *mantra* is certainly no false statement; it is recited with the mouth and contemplated with the mind.

To forget the direct transcendence of the gradual path is a pity, for in these degenerate times, some treat the True Word (mantra) as a mere external technique—whether by chanting over talismans and water, or over medicinal herbs, or even over corpses and ghosts, down to chanting over wood, stone, and poisonous insects—all of which appear to produce results.

If one is truly a follower of the Mantra School (Shingon), there is no hindrance to entering the gateway of *dhāraṇī* and opening the treasury of the Buddha.
This is because it is knowledge and vision; therefore, one who knows the Mantra School (Shingon) knows that this very dharani is it.

That the aforementioned five schools are subsumed within this single gate is due to the fact that the Dharma abides in its own place and the banner of the Dharma is established wherever it may be; it is certainly not a forced assertion.
For one who recognizes the Dharma naturally does not cling to specific gateways nor monopolize a particular school’s tenets. Thus it is said: "One..."
The immeasurable becomes immeasurable; within the small, the great appears, and within the great, the small appears.
Within a single hair-tip, one manifests a jewel-king realm, and while sitting inside a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel. There is nothing that does not manifest spontaneously;
how could one be obstructed by names and words? Aha! The power of the mantra is truly great! How can one not devote one’s whole heart to it?
